title: Coral and the Hymn
premise: Tamsin Halloran, a property surveyor sent to appraise Marsh Hollow's derelict vicarage, discovers the house catalogues its own contents — and its dead. When the village's church bell, melted down in 1911, rings across the marsh, Tamsin is drawn into a covenant the villagers have kept since 1974: each harvest, something is taken from a family and given to the house in exchange for the village's survival. The 'something' taken that year was a child, Coral, whose hymn still echoes through the walls. To end it, Tamsin must find what was physically taken in 1974 — Coral's bones, sealed beneath the new bell's foundation stone — and return them to consecrated ground before the harvest moon rises. He succeeds at terrible cost: the village's protection dies with the covenant, Coral's spirit is freed, and Tamsin, changed by what the house showed him, becomes the hollow's reluctant keeper of the truth.
about_author: Edmund Thackeray is the pen name of a former rural planning officer who spent fifteen years surveying condemned properties across the English fenlands. His debut novel draws on the houses he was never allowed to write reports about.

chapters.title: The Appraisal
chapters.summary: Tamsin arrives at Marsh Hollow to appraise the derelict vicarage, noting details no empty house should have: fresh footprints, a warm hearth, a ledger listing occupants back to 1830. His POV establishes his decade-long habit of rationalizing noises. The beat is unease dressed as professionalism.

chapters.title: Village Records
chapters.summary: In the parish office, Tamsin finds the 1911 record of the bell's melting and a 1974 newspaper clipping about a missing girl, Coral Vane, never found. The clerk, Mrs. Aldous, warns him off the vicarage with practiced blandness. POV Tamsin; the emotional beat is the first crack in his skepticism.

chapters.title: The Bell Rings
chapters.summary: At dusk, a bell tolls though the church tower holds only an empty frame. The village goes silent, doors closing in sequence like a held breath. Tamsin follows the sound to the vicarage door, which opens for him. POV Tamsin; the beat is dread overtaking denial.

chapters.title: The House That Catalogues
chapters.summary: Inside, rooms rearrange around Tamsin, and the ledger now bears his name under tonight's date. He hears a child humming a hymn through the walls. POV Tamsin, intercut with fragments of the house's own 'memory' voice. The beat is the loss of the observer's safety.

chapters.title: Mrs. Aldous Explains Nothing
chapters.summary: Tamsin confronts the clerk, who reveals only that the village pays a tithe every harvest and that he arrived on the wrong year to be a bystander. Her fear is older than her grief. POV Tamsin; the beat is the horror of complicity wrapped in politeness.

chapters.title: Coral's Hymn
chapters.summary: Following the humming, Tamsin finds a child's bedroom preserved mid-1974, and the hymn resolves into words: a plea to be brought home. The room reacts to him, warming, hopeful. POV alternates Tamsin and Coral's fragmented memory. The beat is pity sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Mrs. Aldous's brother, Tom, one of the 1974 tithe-takers, drunkenly tells Tamsin they took more than the girl — they took her from the churchyard where she'd been secretly buried, because the house demanded a body already given to God. POV Tom then Tamsin. The beat is guilt as contagion.

chapters.title: The Foundation Stone
chapters.summary: Tamsin inspects the church and finds the replacement bell's foundation stone, laid 1974, too fresh in the mortar's memory. Beneath it, something answers when he knocks. POV Tamsin; the beat is the dawning geometry of the task: return what was taken.

chapters.title: First Refusal
chapters.summary: The village council, led by squire Edwin Vane — Coral's father — refuses exhumation, threatening Tamsin with the same lawlessness that protected them for fifty years. POV Edwin reveals his corrupted logic: the covenant saved everyone else. The beat is power defending itself.

chapters.title: The House Makes an Offer
chapters.summary: The vicarage offers Tamsin a trade: leave now, forget, be paid handsomely — the same offer accepted by every surveyor before him. He finds their names in the ledger, all crossed out later. POV Tamsin; the beat is temptation and the discovery that refusal has a price.

chapters.title: Night of the Long Tithe
chapters.summary: As the moon waxes, the house grows hungry, taking small things: Tamsin's reflection, his voice for an hour, a villager's newborn's cry. The village begins to fracture. POV shifts among three villagers. The beat is collective dread turning toward blame.

chapters.title: Tom's Confession
chapters.summary: Tom, dying of what the house is reclaiming, gives Tamsin the 1974 tithe ledger page naming every participant, including young Edwin. He begs to be remembered honestly. POV Tom; the beat is confession as the last dignity of the guilty.

chapters.title: Digging by Daylight
chapters.summary: Tamsin and Mrs. Aldous begin covert excavation at the foundation stone, hampered by villagers who watch and do nothing — until one boy helps silently. POV Tamsin; the beat is fragile alliance against a whole town's silence.

chapters.title: Edwin's Bargain
chapters.summary: Edwin offers Tamsin a substitute: another child, a traveler's kid no one will miss, to renew the covenant cleanly. Tamsin refuses and realizes Edwin must never let the truth surface. POV Edwin; the beat is corruption fully articulated — survival as license.

chapters.title: The House Turns
chapters.summary: Denied its renewal, the house stops pretending: walls breathe, the hymn becomes a scream, and the ledger writes Tamsin's death date. He barely escapes at dawn. POV Tamsin; the beat is terror without any remaining ambiguity.

chapters.title: Harvest Moon Rising
chapters.summary: With two nights left, the excavation is exposed; the mob seals the churchyard and locks Tamsin in the vicarage as the tithe's fallback. Coral's presence shields him — the house cannot take what she claims. POV Tamsin and Coral; the beat is solidarity between the living and the taken.

chapters.title: The Village Breaks
chapters.summary: Mrs. Aldous reads Tom's ledger aloud in the church, forcing the village to hear fifty years of names. Half the town turns on Edwin; the seal on the churchyard breaks in the chaos. POV Mrs. Aldous; the beat is truth as a weapon that wounds its wielders too.

chapters.title: The Stone Lifted
chapters.summary: Under the rising harvest moon, Tamsin, the boy, and defected villagers lift the foundation stone and uncover a small coffin. The house convulses, the melted bell ringing from nowhere, closer each peal. POV Tamsin; the beat is desperate, physical labor against supernatural fury.

chapters.title: Return What Was Taken
chapters.summary: They carry Coral home to the old churchyard grave as the house tears itself apart trying to keep her, offering Tamsin visions of everything he's lost to make him stop. He walks through them. POV Tamsin; the beat is grief chosen over comfort.

chapters.title: The Last Peal
chapters.summary: Coral is reburied in consecrated ground as the moon crests; the phantom bell rings once, sweetly, and falls silent forever. The house exhales into ordinary ruin. Edwin, abandoned, walks into the marsh. POV Coral, finally clear; the beat is release.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Weeks later, the village mourns honestly for the first time since 1974, uneasy without its covenant but free. Tamsin files a final appraisal describing the vicarage as uninhabitable, and means it in every sense. POV Tamsin; the beat is survivor's quiet and the cost made visible.

chapters.title: The New Keeper
chapters.summary: Leaving Marsh Hollow, Tamsin finds Coral's hymnbook in his car, a page marked for him — the house, diminished but alive, has named its next warden. He turns toward the horizon, book beside him, not yet deciding. POV Tamsin; the beat is an ending that keeps one door open.
